lesson_title: Day 8 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 7 (the CoinJoin trace lab: where the trace stops and what still shows)

lectures.title: CoinJoin trace lab: where the trace stops

questions.question_stem: Two of the five inputs to a 5x5 equal-output round are the ransom's. What can the analyst say about the five outputs?
questions.correct_answer: Two of them are the ransom's, but which two cannot be told, so the trace stops at a set of five.
incorrect_answers: The first two outputs are the ransom's, because outputs are listed in the order of inputs.
All five are the ransom's, because co-spend puts every input of one transaction in one wallet.
None are the ransom's, because a CoinJoin round breaks the link between its inputs and outputs.
questions.explanation: Equal outputs make the coins interchangeable, so an output cannot be matched to its input. Co-spend does not apply, because the other inputs belong to other people. A CoinJoin stop takes no confidence word: it is the transaction's shape, not a judgment about an owner.

questions.question_stem: The attacker later spends one mixed output together with a coin from the toxic change in one transaction. What does the trace gain?
questions.correct_answer: A post-mix co-spend: the mixed output rejoins the ransom cluster at Moderate, unless it is a PayJoin.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because a mixed coin cannot be linked again to the coins it was mixed with in the round.
A High link, because spending two coins together counts as two independent kinds of evidence, not one.
A second CoinJoin round, because any transaction with two inputs and two outputs mixes the coins it spends.
questions.explanation: Spending mixed coins together with unmixed change undoes the mix. By co-spend one wallet holds all the inputs, so the mixed output is the ransom's. The known false positive is a PayJoin, where the payee adds an input of their own. One heuristic gives Moderate.

questions.question_stem: A mixed output is sent back to the original ransom address, and the transaction carries a taunt in its OP_RETURN field. What confidence does the address reuse get?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate: the reuse is one line of evidence, and the note is text its builder chose, not a second kind of evidence.
incorrect_answers: High: the reuse and the note are two independent kinds of evidence that agree with each other on the owner.
Low: an address can be paid by anyone, so a payment to it says nothing about who owns the address in question.
Moderate: the taunt names the attacker, so the address belongs to the one who wrote that note into the transaction record.
questions.explanation: CoinJoin wallets give a new address every time, so a coin returned to a known address is the user's mistake. Anyone can pay any address, but one output of the whole amount makes that unlikely. A note fits the reading without adding an independent line.

questions.question_stem: Five of eight outputs of a CoinJoin round move within one block, and one moves ten blocks later. May the analyst call the late mover the ransom's?
questions.correct_answer: No: it is a lead at Low, because a careful owner may wait or remix, and any of the eight could move last.
incorrect_answers: Yes, at Moderate: the one that moves last is the one whose owner is most careful, so it is the attacker's.
Yes, at High: moving at a different time from the other seven is very unlikely to be down to chance.
No: timing is not recorded on a chain, so the analyst cannot compare when the eight outputs moved.
questions.explanation: Timing alone is behavior, and behavior is Low. The owner may be waiting for low fees or a purchase, remixing, offline or simply holding. The timing tell is worth following as a lead; it is not a finding.

questions.question_stem: The ransom's coin enters a mixer. Its batch payout has two withdrawals that fit the deposit, less 1.0% and less 2.0%. Why does this cap the confidence?
questions.correct_answer: Neither can be picked: a pool pays amounts that could match any deposit, so each is only a Low lead.
incorrect_answers: The smaller fee is the match, since a mixer charges every customer the same rate, so the first is Moderate.
The mixer's label settles it, since a service that mixes names its customers' withdrawals, so both are High.
Both belong to the attacker, since two matches double the evidence, so the pair is rated as one Moderate.
questions.explanation: A mixer's fee can be any rate, can vary by customer and can be taken in several withdrawals, and its pool mixes many deposits. A matching amount narrows little. The mixer label itself is one unverified label, also Low.
questions.lesson_block: Why a mixer's payout caps confidence
